questions.prompt: A continuous-time linear system \(\dot x = Ax\) is asymptotically stable when
options: every eigenvalue of \(A\) has a negative real part
at least one eigenvalue has a negative real part
the trace of \(A\) is negative, with no other condition
every eigenvalue has a positive real part
questions.explanation: Asymptotic stability needs the whole spectrum in the open left half-plane. One stable eigenvalue does not rescue an unstable partner. A negative trace is necessary for a second-order system but not sufficient. Positive real parts are the unstable case.

questions.prompt: The polynomial \(s^2 + 3s + 2\) has two real roots. The one closer to the imaginary axis is
questions.explanation: \(s^2 + 3s + 2 = (s+1)(s+2)\). The roots are \(-1\) and \(-2\). The slower one is -1. Reporting \(-2\) names the faster pole. Reporting \(+1\) flips the stable sign.

questions.figure_alt: Two pole marks on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: For \(s^3 + 4s^2 + 6s + 4\), the Routh quantity \(ab - c\) (with \(a = 4\), \(b = 6\), \(c = 4\)) is
questions.explanation: The third-order test needs \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) positive and \(ab > c\). Here \(ab - c = 24 - 4 = 20\), so this polynomial passes. The product \(ab = 24\) forgets to subtract \(c\). The difference \(a - c = 0\) is not the Hurwitz minor.

questions.figure_alt: Two pole marks on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: Poles lie at \(-1 \pm j5\) and at \(-8\). The time constant of the slowest mode is
questions.explanation: The real parts are \(-1\) and \(-8\). The slowest decay is \(e^{-t}\), so the time constant is \(1/1 = 1\) s. The fast time constant is \(1/8\). The imaginary part 5 is an oscillation rate, not a time constant.

questions.prompt: A transfer function is BIBO stable while a state-space realization of it is not asymptotically stable when
options: every pole and every eigenvalue is in the open left half-plane
a right-half-plane eigenvalue is cancelled and does not appear as a pole of \(G(s)\)
questions.explanation: Cancellation hides a mode from the input-output map. If that mode is unstable, the transfer function can be BIBO stable while the internal state still runs away. A minimal realization has no such hidden mode, so the two stability notions agree. A sinusoid input does not create a hidden eigenvalue.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a right-half-plane pole</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="147" y2="90"/><line x1="175" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="156" y1="85" x2="166" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="156" y1="95" x2="166" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A pole mark on the positive real axis.

questions.prompt: The polynomial \(s^2 + 1.5 s - 1\) has one root with a positive real part. That unstable root is
questions.explanation: \((s+2)(s-0.5) = s^2 + 1.5s - 1\). The positive root is 0.5. The stable root \(-2\) is the other factor. The coefficient 1.5 is the sum of the root magnitudes with a sign pattern, not the unstable root itself.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a right-half-plane pole</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="147" y2="90"/><line x1="175" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="156" y1="85" x2="166" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="156" y1="95" x2="166" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A pole mark on the positive real axis.

questions.prompt: Simple poles on the imaginary axis, and no poles in the right half-plane, mean the free response is
options: identically zero for every initial state
questions.explanation: A simple pair at \(\pm j\omega\) produces a sustained sinusoid. The state stays bounded and does not return to the origin, so the system is not asymptotically stable. Growth would require a positive real part, or a repeated imaginary pole. The zero response is only the zero initial state.

questions.figure_alt: A conjugate pair on the imaginary axis.

questions.prompt: The polynomial is \(s^3 + 2s^2 + 3s + k\), with \(k > 0\). The Routh boundary \(ab = c\) is crossed at \(k =\)
questions.explanation: Here \(a = 2\) and \(b = 3\), so \(ab = 6\). The constant term \(k\) must stay below 6. The sum \(a + b = 5\) is not the critical value. The product \(a b c\) cannot be formed until \(k\) is known, and it is not the test.

questions.figure_alt: A conjugate pair on the imaginary axis.

questions.prompt: Poles sit at \(-0.2 \pm j4\). Their damping ratio \(\zeta = |\sigma|/\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \omega^2}\) is
questions.explanation: The natural frequency is \(\sqrt{0.2^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{16.04}\), and \(\zeta = 0.2/\sqrt{16.04} = 0.0499376\). Using the imaginary part 4 as \(\zeta\) confuses frequency with a ratio. Using \(0.2/4 = 0.05\) is close, and it drops the real part inside the square root.

questions.figure_alt: A conjugate pair close to the imaginary axis.

questions.prompt: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\). The eigenvalue closer to the imaginary axis is
questions.explanation: The matrix is triangular, so the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries \(-1\) and \(-3\). The slower one is -1. The off-diagonal 4 is not an eigenvalue. The faster pole \(-3\) is the other diagonal entry.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>an upper-triangular state matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-1   4</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   -3</text></svg>

questions.prompt: The Routh-Hurwitz test is used instead of the quadratic formula when
options: the polynomial is first order and the root is obvious
a root is already known to be positive
one only needs to know whether every root is in the open left half-plane, not the root values
questions.explanation: Routh reads stability from the coefficients, which is what a design sweep wants. A first-order polynomial does not need it. The test is for linear characteristic polynomials, not for nonlinear vector fields. A known positive root already answers the stability question.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that settles to a constant.

questions.prompt: For \(s^3 + 5s^2 + 8s + 6\), the Routh quantity \(ab - c\) is
questions.explanation: \(a = 5\), \(b = 8\), \(c = 6\), so \(ab - c = 40 - 6 = 34\). All three coefficients are positive and this minor is positive, so the polynomial is stable. The product \(ab = 40\) forgets to subtract \(c\). The sum of the coefficients, 19, is not the Hurwitz minor.
